Please polish the following text to make it more eloquent and professional, keeping all original information unchanged:

BANGKOK, Thailand (CNN) -- Thailand's military has denied abusing refugee boat-people from Myanmar after claims some were whipped on a tourist beach and hundreds more left dead or missing after being towed at to sea without food and water. Photograph released by Thai navy showing a group of illegal immigrants captured on December 12. Photos showing refugees being made to lie face down on a popular beach and media reports claiming refugees been deliberately lost at sea have sparked concerns for their safety. The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees says it is "concerned" about the fate of the Muslim ethnic minority Rohingya people, who have fled from Myanmar's border with Bangladesh. The agency says it has written a formal note to the Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs asking for clarification of what is happening. CNN spoke to one Australian tourist, who declined to be named for fear of being barred from Thailand, who says boat-people were "whipped" by Thai guards on popular diving resort island in the Similan Archipelago last month. Local media also report claims by Rohingya survivors that the Thai military have been detaining hundreds of them an island called Koh Sai Daeng before towing them back out into open water without supplies. The survivors say hundreds of them drowned and only the lucky ones made it to the Indian Andaman Islands or Indonesia's Aceh province. The Thai Navy denies knowledge of the incident. Rear Admiral Naris Pratumsuwan told CNN "as a normal practice, if Navy finds illegal immigrants, we will hand them over to related authorities, e.g. police or immigration police." He said he had not received any information on an island where migrants are being detained. There were reports of another boatload of 46 Rohingya detained by the Thai military Friday, but there was no official confirmation. The Rohingya have been fleeing persecution of the hard-line military regime in Myanmar, formerly Burma, for years and often seek refuge in Malaysia. Boat loads of Rohingya arriving in Thailand is nothing new, but non-governmental organizations are increasingly worried about what they say is an apparent change of government policy. They say the army's Internal Security Operations Command is forcing the Rohingya out to sea rather than deporting them overland back to Myanmar. "The Thai government is taking highly vulnerable people and risking their lives for political gain," says Refugee International's Sean Garcia says. "It should be engaging the Burmese government on improving conditions at home for the Rohingya if it wants to stem these flows. "The Rohingya will continue to make the journey because they have no hope for a better life in Burma. Pushing them back out to sea is not an effective deterrent it just jeopardizes lives."

outputs.L1:
BANGKOK, Thailand (CNN) — Thailand’s military has denied abusing refugee boat people from Myanmar, following allegations that some were whipped on a tourist beach and that hundreds more were left dead or missing after being towed out to sea without food or water.

A photograph released by the Thai navy shows a group of illegal immigrants captured on December 12. Images of refugees being forced to lie face down on a popular beach, along with media reports claiming that refugees had been deliberately abandoned at sea, have raised concerns for their safety.

The United Nations High Commissioner for Refugees says it is “concerned” about the fate of the Rohingya, a Muslim ethnic minority who have fled Myanmar’s border region with Bangladesh. The agency says it has sent a formal note to the Thai Ministry of Foreign Affairs requesting clarification about what is happening.

CNN spoke to one Australian tourist, who declined to be named for fear of being barred from Thailand, who said boat people were “whipped” by Thai guards on a popular diving-resort island in the Similan Archipelago last month.

Local media have also reported claims by Rohingya survivors that the Thai military had detained hundreds of them on an island called Koh Sai Daeng before towing them back out into open water without supplies. The survivors said hundreds of them drowned, and that only the lucky ones reached India’s Andaman Islands or Indonesia’s Aceh province.

The Thai navy has denied knowledge of the incident. Rear Admiral Naris Pratumsuwan told CNN, “As a normal practice, if the navy finds illegal immigrants, we will hand them over to the relevant authorities, such as the police or immigration police.” He said he had not received any information about an island where migrants were being detained.

There were reports Friday of another boatload of 46 Rohingya being detained by the Thai military, but there was no official confirmation.

The Rohingya have been fleeing persecution by Myanmar’s hard-line military regime, formerly known as Burma, for years and often seek refuge in Malaysia. Boatloads of Rohingya arriving in Thailand are not new, but nongovernmental organizations are increasingly concerned about what they describe as an apparent shift in government policy.

They say the army’s Internal Security Operations Command is forcing the Rohingya out to sea rather than deporting them overland back to Myanmar.

“The Thai government is taking highly vulnerable people and risking their lives for political gain,” said Refugees International’s Sean Garcia. “It should be engaging the Burmese government on improving conditions at home for the Rohingya if it wants to stem these flows.

“The Rohingya will continue to make the journey because they have no hope for a better life in Burma. Pushing them back out to sea is not an effective deterrent; it just jeopardizes lives.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Write a CNN-style news article about Thailand’s military denying allegations that it abused Rohingya boat refugees from Myanmar, including claims they were whipped on a tourist beach and towed out to sea without food or water.
counterfactuals.output:
**Thailand military denies abusing Rohingya boat refugees**

**Bangkok, Thailand** — Thailand’s military has denied allegations that its forces abused Rohingya boat refugees from Myanmar, including claims that migrants were whipped on a beach popular with tourists and later towed back out to sea without adequate food or water.

The accusations have drawn renewed attention to the treatment of Rohingya migrants, a Muslim minority group from Myanmar who have long faced persecution and statelessness. Many have attempted dangerous sea journeys toward Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia in overcrowded wooden boats.

Thai military officials said the allegations were false and insisted that security forces had acted in accordance with national and international obligations. They said authorities provided humanitarian assistance to people found at sea and denied using violence against them.

The denials followed reports from survivors and human rights advocates who alleged that Rohingya men arriving by boat were detained by Thai forces, beaten or whipped, and in some cases taken to remote locations before being pushed back into international waters.

Some accounts alleged that refugees were held on a beach in southern Thailand, an area frequented by tourists, where they were struck by security personnel. Others claimed that boats carrying the migrants were later towed away from shore and released with little or no food, water or fuel.

Human rights groups have called for an independent investigation, saying the claims, if substantiated, would amount to serious abuses against vulnerable refugees and migrants.

“The Thai government must ensure that anyone arriving by sea is treated humanely and given access to protection procedures,” one rights advocate said. “Pushing people back into dangerous waters can have deadly consequences.”

Thai officials have faced international scrutiny in the past over the handling of Rohingya arrivals, particularly during periods when large numbers of people fled Myanmar by sea. Authorities have at times described the arrivals as illegal migration and a national security concern, while humanitarian groups have urged Thailand not to return people to situations where they could face persecution.

The Rohingya are not recognized as citizens by Myanmar, where many have been subjected to restrictions on movement, education, health care and employment. Waves of violence and military crackdowns have forced hundreds of thousands to flee, most notably to Bangladesh, while others continue to seek refuge elsewhere in Southeast Asia.

Thailand is not a signatory to the 1951 U.N. Refugee Convention, but international law prohibits returning people to places where they face serious harm, a principle known as non-refoulement.

The Thai military said it would cooperate with any inquiries ordered by the government, while maintaining that its personnel had not mistreated the migrants.

Humanitarian organizations say the case underscores the need for a regional response to Rohingya migration, including safe disembarkation, screening for protection needs and accountability for abuses at sea.
counterfactuals.label: cf_1

**Bangkok —** The plight of Rohingya refugees in Thailand has drawn renewed international concern amid allegations that some asylum seekers fleeing persecution and poverty in Myanmar and Bangladesh have been intercepted at sea and pushed back or otherwise mistreated.

The United Nations refugee agency, UNHCR, has expressed concern over the fate of Rohingya boat people arriving in Thai waters, urging authorities to ensure that all asylum seekers are given access to protection procedures and humanitarian assistance. UNHCR officials have said they are seeking access to detainees and survivors to assess their needs and determine whether they require international protection.

Thailand’s navy has denied accusations that it has abused Rohingya migrants or forced them back to sea in unsafe conditions. Thai officials have said their forces are acting within the law to combat people-smuggling networks and prevent irregular migration, while providing basic assistance when necessary. The navy has rejected claims that refugees were abandoned without adequate food, water or navigation equipment.

Survivors, however, have described a different account. Some Rohingya who reached shore or were rescued after days at sea have claimed that Thai security forces detained them, beat them, and towed their boats away from the coast before cutting them adrift. They said many on board were weak from hunger and dehydration, and that some passengers died during the journey.

Human rights advocates say the allegations fit a broader pattern of regional neglect toward the Rohingya, a Muslim minority long denied citizenship and basic rights in Myanmar. Refugees International has criticized Thailand’s handling of the crisis, calling on the government to stop any pushbacks, allow UNHCR full access to Rohingya detainees, and investigate claims of abuse by security forces.

The organization has also urged neighboring governments and regional bodies to address the root causes of Rohingya displacement and to crack down on trafficking networks without punishing refugees.

Thailand has historically treated Rohingya arrivals as illegal migrants rather than refugees, since it is not a party to the 1951 Refugee Convention. But rights groups argue that Bangkok remains bound by international norms, including the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning people to places where they may face persecution or serious harm.

The latest allegations have placed Thailand under growing scrutiny as governments across Southeast Asia struggle with the movement of Rohingya by sea. Aid agencies warn that without safe landing, screening and protection mechanisms, more refugees could die in the Andaman Sea.

**Reports: Rohingya migrants detained on Thai islands, pushed back to sea**

*BANGKOK, Thailand —* Thai authorities detained hundreds of Rohingya migrants on remote islands before towing them back into open water in boats with little food, water or fuel, according to survivor accounts and human rights groups, raising fears that scores of people may have died or disappeared at sea.

The migrants, members of a Muslim minority group that has long fled persecution and poverty in Myanmar, were reportedly intercepted after arriving in Thailand by boat. Witnesses and rights advocates said some were held on isolated islands before being forced back into the Andaman Sea.

Survivors later found in India and Indonesia described being placed aboard engineless or disabled boats and set adrift. Some said Thai security personnel beat migrants and removed engines from their vessels before towing them away from shore.

Human rights organizations have called for an investigation, saying the accounts suggest a coordinated “push-back” policy that may have violated international law.

Thai officials have denied wrongdoing or said authorities were attempting to prevent illegal migration and human smuggling. Some officials acknowledged intercepting boats but disputed allegations that migrants were intentionally abandoned at sea.

The reported incidents have drawn renewed attention to the plight of the Rohingya, who are denied citizenship in Myanmar and often travel through dangerous maritime routes seeking work or refuge in Thailand, Malaysia and Indonesia.

Aid agencies say the journey is frequently organized by smugglers and can take weeks. Boats are often overcrowded and poorly supplied, leaving passengers vulnerable to starvation, dehydration and drowning.

Survivors’ accounts indicate that many passengers did not reach land. Rights groups said the number of missing remains unclear, but they fear dozens — possibly hundreds — may have died.

The allegations have prompted calls from international organizations for Thailand to grant access to detained migrants, allow independent monitors to investigate, and ensure that asylum seekers are not returned to situations where their lives may be at risk.

Thailand has long served as a transit point for Rohingya migrants, many of whom seek to continue onward to Malaysia. But the country has not signed the 1951 U.N. Refugee Convention, and migrants intercepted at sea are often treated as illegal entrants.

Regional governments have faced increasing pressure to address the Rohingya crisis, particularly during periods when large numbers of boats leave Myanmar and Bangladesh after the monsoon season.

Rights advocates say the latest reports underscore a broader failure by Southeast Asian governments to protect vulnerable migrants at sea.

“Pushing people back into open water without supplies is not border control,” one advocate said. “It is a death sentence.”

counterfactuals.prompt: Draft a detailed breaking-news piece about Myanmar Rohingya boat people arriving in Thailand, allegations of mistreatment by Thai military forces, and the government’s response.
counterfactuals.output:
**BREAKING NEWS: Rohingya Boat People Land in Thailand Amid Allegations of Mistreatment by Military Forces**

**BANGKOK —** A group of Rohingya boat people has arrived on Thailand’s southern coast, renewing scrutiny of the country’s handling of refugees and migrants fleeing persecution and hardship in Myanmar and Bangladesh, as rights groups and survivors allege mistreatment by Thai military personnel.

Thai authorities confirmed that a boat carrying Rohingya men, women and children was found near the coast after reportedly spending days at sea. Officials said the passengers were taken into custody for health checks, identification and immigration processing. The exact number of people on board and their point of departure were not immediately clear.

The arrival comes amid fresh allegations that Thai security forces have subjected Rohingya boat people to harsh treatment, including detention in poor conditions, intimidation, and in some cases being pushed back to sea. Human rights advocates say such actions, if confirmed, would violate Thailand’s obligations under international humanitarian norms, including the principle of non-refoulement, which prohibits returning people to places where they may face persecution or serious harm.

Survivors and advocates allege that some Rohingya arrivals have been held by military or border-security units before being transferred to immigration authorities. In accounts relayed through local aid workers, passengers described exhaustion, dehydration and fear after long journeys aboard overcrowded vessels. Some said they had fled worsening conditions in Myanmar’s Rakhine State or refugee camps in Bangladesh, where many Rohingya have lived for years with limited rights, restricted movement and few prospects for resettlement.

Thai military officials have denied wrongdoing, saying security forces are acting in accordance with national law and humanitarian procedures. Government representatives said authorities are providing food, water and medical screening to those found at sea or along the coast, while also working to combat human trafficking networks that profit from the Rohingya’s desperation.

“The government is committed to humane treatment while protecting national security and enforcing immigration law,” a Thai official said, adding that any credible complaint of abuse would be reviewed by relevant agencies.

The Thai government also said it is coordinating with local authorities, international organizations and neighboring countries to determine the next steps for the group. However, officials did not immediately say whether the new arrivals would be permitted to apply for protection, transferred to immigration detention centers, or treated as victims of trafficking.

Rights groups are urging Bangkok to allow immediate access to the group by the United Nations refugee agency, medical teams and independent monitors. Advocates warn that without transparency, Rohingya arrivals risk indefinite detention, forced return, or exploitation by smugglers and traffickers operating across maritime routes in the Andaman Sea.

The Rohingya, a mostly Muslim minority from Myanmar, have faced decades of discrimination and statelessness. Hundreds of thousands fled to Bangladesh after a brutal military crackdown in Myanmar in 2017, which the United Nations and human rights organizations have described as involving mass killings, sexual violence and village burnings. Myanmar has rejected accusations of genocide, while many Rohingya remain unable to safely return home.

Thailand has long been a transit point for Rohingya attempting to reach Malaysia or Indonesia, where many hope to find work or reunite with relatives. But sea journeys are perilous, especially during the sailing season when traffickers often cram passengers onto unsafe boats with limited food, water and fuel. Regional governments have repeatedly faced criticism for pushbacks and for failing to establish a coordinated protection system.

The latest landing is likely to intensify pressure on Thailand’s government, which has sought to balance border enforcement with international expectations over refugee protection. Humanitarian organizations say the immediate priority must be to ensure that the new arrivals are not punished for seeking safety.

“People fleeing persecution and life-threatening conditions should not be treated as criminals,” one rights advocate said. “Thailand should provide safe disembarkation, medical care, protection screening and access to asylum procedures.”

As of late Tuesday, authorities had not released a full list of those aboard the vessel or details about their condition. Journalists and independent observers were not immediately granted access to the group.

The situation remains developing.

counterfactuals.prompt: Create a factual news summary covering allegations that Thailand’s army and navy abused Rohingya refugees, including tourist eyewitness accounts from the Similan Islands, media reports, and NGO reactions.
counterfactuals.output:
Thailand’s military faced serious allegations of abusing Rohingya refugees after reports emerged that army and navy personnel detained boat people, beat them, and forced some back out to sea in unsafe vessels.

The allegations centered on Rohingya Muslims fleeing persecution and poverty in Myanmar’s Rakhine State. Several media reports said groups of Rohingya migrants who landed in southern Thailand were intercepted by Thai security forces, held on beaches or islands, and in some cases towed into international waters with little food, water, or working engines. Survivors later rescued near India and Indonesia alleged that Thai forces had removed or disabled boat engines before abandoning them at sea.

Tourists in the Similan Islands, a popular diving destination off Thailand’s Andaman coast, also reported witnessing mistreatment. Eyewitness accounts described seeing Rohingya men held under guard on beaches, appearing exhausted and underfed. Some tourists said Thai military personnel struck or kicked detainees and kept them confined in harsh conditions before they were taken away. The accounts drew attention because they came from foreign visitors in a well-known tourist area rather than from remote border zones.

International media outlets, including the BBC, CNN, and regional newspapers, reported on the claims, publishing survivor testimony and photographs that appeared to show Rohingya men being detained by Thai forces. The reports suggested that Thailand had used a “push-back” policy against Rohingya arrivals, treating them as illegal migrants rather than asylum seekers or trafficking victims. Thai officials gave mixed responses, with some denying abuse and others acknowledging that migrants had been intercepted and removed from Thai waters. Authorities said they were trying to prevent illegal entry and human smuggling.

Human rights organizations condemned the alleged actions. Amnesty International, Human Rights Watch, and other NGOs called for an independent investigation, saying that towing people out to sea without adequate supplies could amount to inhumane treatment and violate international obligations. Refugee advocates urged Thailand to grant the Rohingya access to the UN refugee agency and to screen them for protection needs instead of summarily expelling them.

The controversy intensified scrutiny of Thailand’s handling of Rohingya refugees and boat migrants. NGOs argued that the episode reflected a broader regional failure to protect Rohingya people, who often lack citizenship in Myanmar and face discrimination, restrictions on movement, and periodic violence. They called on Thailand and neighboring countries to stop push-backs, investigate military abuses, and cooperate on humane rescue and asylum procedures.
